title: Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill
bigQuestion: How do four habits keep food from making people sick?

story.title: The Potato Salad in the Sun
story.kicker: The family picnic had everything: a grill, a big cooler, and one bowl that nobody put away.
paragraphs: Marcus's aunt made the potato salad the night before. She boiled the potatoes, mixed in the mayonnaise, eggs and celery, covered the bowl and put it in the fridge. At the park the next day she set it on the picnic table at eleven in the morning, next to the buns and the chips. It was the first hot Saturday of June, and the thermometer on the shelter wall read 92 °F.

Uncle Ray ran the grill. He had a thermometer in his apron pocket and used it on every burger. "One-sixty," he said, showing Marcus the dial. "Ground beef has to hit 160. Chicken has to hit 165." He used one plate to carry raw patties out and a different clean plate to carry cooked ones back. Marcus thought that was a lot of fuss for a burger.

People ate lunch around noon. Then there was a softball game, then a second round of burgers around three. The potato salad was still on the table. The bowl was warm to the touch. Marcus's cousin Dee took a big spoonful. Marcus, who had been eating chips, did not.

By Sunday morning Dee and two other cousins were sick, with cramps and a fever. Marcus's aunt was upset. "I made it fresh," she said. "It was in the fridge all night." Uncle Ray shook his head. "It was not the fridge," he said. "It was the four hours on that table in the sun."

Later, Marcus looked up the rule. Food that should be cold cannot sit out more than two hours. When the air is above 90 °F, that drops to one hour. The salad had sat for four. Bacteria too small to see had been growing in it the whole afternoon, and nothing about the taste or smell gave them away.
story.think: Uncle Ray's burgers did not make anyone sick and the potato salad did. What did he do that nobody did for the salad?

lessons.title: Germs That Grow in Food
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria you cannot see, taste or smell grow in food and cause most foodborne illness.
reading: Picture a container of leftover rice left on the counter overnight. In the morning it looks fine. It smells fine. It would taste fine. Yet a spoonful of it can hold millions of *bacteria*, living cells far too small to see, and some of them make poisons that cause vomiting and cramps. Food that makes you sick almost never looks spoiled. That is what makes it dangerous.

Bacteria need four things to multiply: food, moisture, warmth and time. Cooked rice, meat, eggs, dairy, cut fruit and cooked vegetables give them the first two. A warm room gives them the third. Every hour on the counter gives them the fourth. Under good conditions one cell can split into two about every twenty minutes, so a small number becomes a huge number in a few hours.

Sickness from food is called *foodborne illness*. Common causes include Salmonella, often found on raw poultry and eggs, and E. coli, linked to undercooked ground beef and unwashed produce. Symptoms may take hours or days to show up, so the meal that made you sick is often not the last one you ate.

You cannot see bacteria, so you cannot check food by looking. Instead, you control the four things they need. The rest of this chapter is four habits that do exactly that: clean, separate, cook and chill. Learn them once and you will use them for the rest of your life.

words.d: living cells too small to see; some kinds spoil food or cause illness
sickness caused by eating food that carries harmful germs or their poisons

look.title: The Rice on the Counter
look.text: A pot of rice was cooked at 6 p.m. and left on the stove with the lid on. At 8 a.m. it looks and smells exactly the same as it did last night. Someone says, "It's fine, it was covered." Think about the four things bacteria need and which ones the rice gave them overnight.
look.prompt: Explain why the lid did not protect the rice, and what should have happened at 8 p.m.

check.q: Which of these tells you food is safe to eat?
choices: It was kept cold and cooked to the right temperature
check.why: Harmful bacteria do not change the look, smell or taste of food. Only handling tells you it is safe.

check.q: What four things do bacteria need to multiply?
check.why: Bacteria need food, moisture, warmth and time. Food safety habits take away warmth and time.

check.q: Why is the last meal you ate not always the one that made you sick?
choices: Bacteria only grow in breakfast foods
Symptoms can take hours or days to appear
Sickness always comes from restaurant food
Only raw food can carry bacteria
check.why: Foodborne illness can show up hours or days later, so an earlier meal is often the cause.

lessons.title: The Danger Zone
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria grow fastest between 40 and 140 °F, so keep cold food cold and hot food hot.
reading: Open a refrigerator and put a thermometer inside. It should read 40 °F or lower. Now think about a pot of soup on the stove, steaming at well over 140 °F. Between those two numbers is the *danger zone*: 40 to 140 °F. In that range, bacteria multiply quickly. Below it they slow down; above it they die off as food cooks.

Almost every room in a house sits inside the danger zone. A kitchen at 72 °F is right in the middle of it. That is why the counter is the worst place to keep food that needs to stay cold or hot. The fridge is below the zone. A hot oven or a warming tray is above it. The table at a picnic is inside it, and on a summer day it is deep inside it.

The fridge works only when it is truly cold. Set it at or below 40 °F and check it with a small fridge thermometer, because the dial on the door does not show degrees. The freezer should read 0 °F. Freezing does not kill bacteria; it stops them from growing. When frozen food thaws into the zone, they start growing again.

Keeping food out of the zone is the idea behind most of the rules you will learn. Chill leftovers fast. Cook meat all the way. Do not thaw on the counter. Each rule is one way of moving food through 40 to 140 °F as quickly as possible, or keeping it out entirely.

words.d: 40 to 140 °F, the temperature range where bacteria grow fastest
a small thermometer kept inside the refrigerator to check that it stays at or below 40 °F

look.title: Temperatures a Cook Should Know
look.cite: USDA and FDA food safety guidance
look.prompt: A kitchen at 72 °F sits inside the danger zone. Where would you keep a bowl of cut melon before lunch, and why?

check.q: What is the danger zone?
check.why: The danger zone is 40 to 140 °F, where bacteria multiply fastest.

check.q: What temperature should a refrigerator hold?
check.why: A refrigerator should be at or below 40 °F, just under the danger zone.

check.q: What does freezing do to bacteria in food?
choices: Stops them from growing until the food thaws
check.why: Freezing at 0 °F stops growth but does not kill bacteria; they resume growing when the food thaws.

lessons.title: The Two-Hour Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Perishable food may sit out two hours at most, or one hour when the air is above 90 °F.
reading: Think of the chicken on the counter after dinner. Dishes take a while, someone gets a phone call, and the chicken sits. The rule is simple: *perishable* food, meaning food that spoils, may stay in the danger zone for no more than two hours total. After that, throw it out. Do not taste it to check. Do not reheat it to fix it. Out.

Two hours is the limit for a normal room. When the air is above 90 °F, at a picnic, in a hot car, or on a porch in July, the limit drops to one hour. Bacteria grow faster in a hotter room, so they use up the safe time faster. The potato salad in the story sat for four hours at 92 °F, four times its limit.

The clock is a running total, not a fresh start. If the milk sat out for an hour at breakfast and an hour at lunch, its two hours are gone. To keep track, set a timer when food comes out of the fridge. A twenty-minute lunch is not a problem. A bowl left out through a whole movie is.

Perishable foods include meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, cooked rice and pasta, cooked vegetables, cut fruit and anything made with them. Dry crackers, whole uncut fruit, bread and unopened cans are not. At a picnic, keep the perishables in a cooler with ice until the moment they are served, then put them back.

words.d: food that spoils and can grow harmful bacteria if it is not kept cold or hot
perishable food can sit in the danger zone for two hours at most, one hour when the air is above 90 °F

look.title: A Day of Small Sit-Outs
look.text: A carton of milk comes out at 7:00 a.m. and goes back at 7:40. It comes out again at 12:00 for lunch and goes back at 12:30. After school it sits on the counter from 3:30 to 4:45 while everyone does homework. Add up the minutes the milk spent in the danger zone.
look.prompt: Has the milk passed the two-hour rule? Show your total and say what you would do with the carton.

check.q: How long may cooked chicken sit out in a 72 °F kitchen?
check.why: The two-hour rule: perishable food gets two hours at most in the danger zone.

check.q: At a picnic where the air is 95 °F, how long may potato salad sit on the table?
check.why: Above 90 °F the limit drops to one hour because bacteria grow faster in heat.

check.q: Food sat out too long. What is the right move?
choices: Reheat it until it is steaming
Put it in the fridge right away
check.why: Reheating does not remove the poisons some bacteria make, and tasting cannot detect them. Throw it out.

lessons.title: Hands and Surfaces
lessons.mainIdea: Wash hands for twenty seconds with soap and water before, during and after handling food.
reading: Stand at the sink. Wet your hands with clean running water, turn the water off, and apply soap. Rub your palms, the backs of your hands, between your fingers and under your nails for a full *twenty seconds*, about the time it takes to hum "Happy Birthday" twice. Rinse under running water and dry with a clean towel or a paper towel. That is a hand wash. Anything shorter is a rinse.

Wash before you start cooking, after touching raw meat, poultry, fish or eggs, after using the bathroom, after touching your face, hair or phone, after handling trash, and after touching a pet. In a cooking lab that means washing several times in one class, and that is normal. Hand sanitizer is a backup for when there is no sink, but it does not remove grease or dirt the way soap does.

Surfaces need the same care. Before you begin, wipe the counter and cutting boards with hot soapy water. After raw meat touches a surface, wash it again with hot soapy water and then *sanitize* it, which means treating it to kill the bacteria that washing left behind. A common home sanitizer is a solution of a small amount of unscented bleach in water; follow the label.

Sponges and dish towels are a hidden problem. A damp sponge is warm, wet and full of food, all four things bacteria want. Use paper towels to clean up raw meat juices, change dish towels often, and let sponges dry out between uses or replace them. Tie back long hair, take off rings and bracelets, and wear an apron, so that you are not adding to the counter what you just cleaned off it.

words.d: the minimum time for scrubbing hands with soap, about two rounds of "Happy Birthday"
to treat a cleaned surface with heat or a chemical to kill the bacteria that washing leaves behind

look.title: Count the Hand Washes
look.text: In one lab a student washes hands, cuts raw chicken into strips, wipes her nose with the back of her hand, checks her phone for the recipe, tears lettuce for the salad, takes the trash bag out, and then plates the cooked chicken with her fingers.
look.prompt: Mark every moment she should have washed her hands again, and count them.

check.q: How long should you scrub with soap when washing your hands?
check.why: Twenty seconds of scrubbing with soap is the standard, about two rounds of "Happy Birthday".

check.q: You just cut raw chicken and now need to tear lettuce. What comes first?
choices: Wash hands with soap for twenty seconds
check.why: Raw poultry carries bacteria; a full soap-and-water wash is needed before touching ready-to-eat food.

check.q: Why is a damp kitchen sponge a problem?
choices: It stays warm, wet and full of food, so bacteria grow in it
check.why: A wet sponge gives bacteria food, moisture, warmth and time. Let it dry or replace it.

lessons.title: Produce and Dishes
lessons.mainIdea: Rinse produce under running water and wash dishes hot, soapy and in order.
reading: Take a head of lettuce and an apple. Even if you will peel the apple, rinse it first under cool running water and rub it with your hands. Otherwise the knife drags whatever is on the peel into the fruit. Pull the lettuce leaves apart and rinse each one, then dry them in a spinner or on a clean towel. Firm produce like potatoes and carrots can be scrubbed with a clean vegetable brush. Do not use soap; produce is not made to be eaten with soap on it.

Rinse produce right before you use it, not before you store it. Wet berries in the fridge grow mold. Cut the bruised or damaged spots away. Packaged salad marked "prewashed" or "ready to eat" does not need another rinse. Melons deserve special care: scrub the rind before cutting, because the knife carries anything on the outside straight through the sweet, wet inside.

Dishes get washed in a set order so the water stays clean as long as possible. Scrape food into the trash first. Fill the sink with hot, soapy water. Wash the least greasy items first: glasses and cups, then silverware, then plates and bowls, then pots and pans, and cutting boards that touched raw meat last of all. Rinse in hot water and let dishes air-dry in a rack, or dry them with a clean towel.

A dishwasher does the same job with hotter water than hands can stand, which is why it is a good place for cutting boards and knives that are dishwasher-safe. Cutting boards with deep knife grooves are hard to clean and should be replaced. Wooden boards should never soak; they crack, and cracks hold bacteria.

words.d: fresh fruits and vegetables
to let washed dishes dry in a rack instead of wiping them, so a towel cannot spread germs

look.title: Order the Dish Pile
look.text: In the sink after a lab: a greasy skillet, four water glasses, the cutting board used for raw chicken, six forks, two dinner plates with sauce on them, and a mixing bowl with a little batter left in it.
look.prompt: Put these in washing order, first to last, and say why the chicken board goes where it goes.

check.q: Why rinse an apple even if you plan to peel it?
choices: The knife carries dirt from the peel into the fruit
Water makes it easier to peel
Peeling does nothing, so rinsing is the only step
check.why: Whatever is on the peel travels on the blade into the flesh, so rinse first.

check.q: Which dishes are washed first in a sink of hot soapy water?
check.why: Wash the least greasy items first so the water stays clean: glasses, then silverware, plates, pots, and raw-meat boards last.

check.q: When should you rinse fresh berries?
choices: Before putting them in the fridge
check.why: Rinse produce just before use. Wet berries stored in the fridge grow mold faster.

lessons.title: Cross-Contamination
lessons.mainIdea: Cross-contamination moves bacteria from raw food to ready-to-eat food; separate keeps them apart.
reading: Picture a cutting board. Someone slices raw chicken on it, sets the chicken in the pan, and then slices tomatoes for a salad on the same board. The chicken is going to be cooked to 165 °F, so its bacteria will die. The tomatoes will not be cooked at all. Every germ the board picked up from the chicken now rides on the salad. This is *cross-contamination*: bacteria moving from one food, surface or hand to another.

Raw meat, poultry, fish and eggs are the usual sources. *Ready-to-eat* foods are the usual victims: salads, fruit, bread, cooked dishes, anything that will not be heated again before it is eaten. The rule is to keep the two groups apart at every stage: in the cart, in the fridge, on the counter, on the plate.

Cross-contamination happens through surfaces, through tools and through hands. A knife used on raw meat and then on cheese. A plate that carried raw burgers to the grill and then the cooked ones back. Tongs that flipped raw chicken and then served the cooked pieces. Hands that touched raw meat and then the fridge handle, the salt shaker and the bag of rolls.

The fix is a separate tool or a wash between uses. Two cutting boards, two plates, two sets of tongs, or one of each washed in hot soapy water in between. Never rinse raw poultry in the sink; the water splashes bacteria onto the counter, the faucet and the dishes nearby. Cooking kills the bacteria on the chicken anyway.

words.d: the spread of bacteria from one food, surface, tool or hand to another
food that will not be cooked before it is eaten, such as salad, fruit or bread

look.title: Find the Cross-Contamination
look.text: Dad cuts raw pork chops on the board, seasons them, and slides them into the oven. He rinses the board under the faucet, sets it back on the counter, and starts chopping cucumbers and peppers for a salad on it. He uses the same knife. Then he grabs the salad tongs from the drawer with the hand that seasoned the pork.
look.prompt: List every place bacteria from the pork could reach the salad, and say what would fix each one.

check.q: What is cross-contamination?
choices: Cooking two foods at the same time
Bacteria spreading from one food, tool or hand to another
Mixing ingredients in the wrong order
check.why: Cross-contamination is the spread of bacteria between foods, surfaces, tools and hands.

check.q: Raw chicken was cut on a board. What happens if you slice tomatoes on it next?
choices: The tomatoes will be fine because chicken bacteria only live in chicken
The tomatoes cook the bacteria away
The board's bacteria move onto tomatoes that will never be cooked
Nothing, if the board is plastic
check.why: The tomatoes are ready-to-eat and will not be cooked, so the chicken bacteria go straight to the plate.

check.q: Why should raw chicken not be rinsed in the sink?
choices: Splashing spreads bacteria around the sink and counter
check.why: Rinsing splashes bacteria onto surfaces; cooking to 165 °F kills them without the rinse.

lessons.title: Boards, Plates and Fridge Order
lessons.mainIdea: Use separate boards and plates for raw meat, and store raw meat on the bottom shelf.
reading: Many kitchens use color-coded cutting boards. One common scheme uses red for raw meat, yellow for raw poultry, blue for fish, and green for produce. Any scheme works as long as everyone in the kitchen uses the same one. At home, two boards are enough: one that only ever sees raw meat, poultry and fish, and one for everything else. Write it on the board if you have to.

Plates and tools follow the same idea. Carry raw burgers to the grill on one plate and bring the cooked burgers back on a clean one. Never put cooked food back on the plate that held it raw. Marinade that soaked raw meat cannot be served as a sauce unless it is boiled first; it is simpler to set some aside before it touches the meat.

The refrigerator has an order too. Raw meat, poultry and fish go on the bottom shelf, on a plate or in a container that catches drips. Ready-to-eat food goes above them. That way a leaking package of chicken drips onto the shelf below, not onto the strawberries. Eggs stay in their carton on a shelf, not in the door, because the door is the warmest spot.

At the store, the same rule applies. Put raw meat in the plastic bags the store provides, keep it apart from produce in the cart, and bag it separately at checkout. On the way home, it should be the last thing in the cart and the first thing in the fridge.

words.d: cutting boards in set colors so raw meat, poultry, fish and produce each get their own board
a seasoned liquid that raw meat soaks in; once it has touched raw meat it must be boiled or thrown out

look.title: Load the Fridge
look.text: Groceries on the counter: a package of raw chicken thighs, a bag of grapes, a carton of eggs, a tub of yogurt, a pound of raw ground beef, a bagged salad, and a package of cooked deli turkey. The fridge has a top shelf, a middle shelf, a bottom shelf, a crisper drawer and door shelves.
look.prompt: Say where each item goes and explain the one rule that decides the bottom shelf.

check.q: Where should raw chicken go in the refrigerator?
choices: On the bottom shelf in a container
check.why: Raw meat goes on the bottom shelf so any drips fall on nothing edible below.

check.q: Raw burgers went out to the grill on a plate. The cooked burgers should come back on what?
choices: The same plate, wiped with a napkin
A paper towel on the same plate
check.why: Cooked food never returns to a plate that held it raw; that is cross-contamination.

check.q: What can you do with marinade that soaked raw chicken if you want it as a sauce?
choices: Serve it as is; the vinegar kills germs
Chill it and serve it cold
Boil it first, or set some aside before it touches the chicken
check.why: Marinade from raw meat carries its bacteria; boiling kills them, or use a portion that never touched the meat.

lessons.title: The Food Thermometer
lessons.mainIdea: Only a thermometer in the thickest part of the food can tell you it has reached a safe temperature.
reading: Cut into a chicken thigh and the juices run clear, so it must be done, right? Not always. Color and juices are unreliable; some poultry stays pink at a safe temperature and some ground beef turns brown before it reaches one. The only way to know is a *food thermometer*. A digital instant-read thermometer costs about the price of a fast-food meal (example) and reads in a few seconds.

To use one, push the probe into the *thickest part* of the food, away from bone, fat and the pan. Bone heats faster than meat and gives a false high reading. For a thin burger, slide the probe in from the side so the tip reaches the middle. For a whole chicken, check the thickest part of the thigh and the thickest part of the breast. Wait for the numbers to stop moving.

Check the thermometer itself now and then. Fill a glass with crushed ice, top it with water, stir, and put the probe in without touching the sides. It should read 32 °F. If it does not, many thermometers have a small nut behind the dial or a reset button to adjust it. A thermometer that reads wrong is worse than none, because it makes you confident.

Wash the probe in hot soapy water after every use, especially between checking raw and cooked food. Pushing a probe that touched raw chicken into a cooked burger is cross-contamination with extra steps. Keep the thermometer where you can reach it; the one in the back of the drawer never gets used.

words.d: a probe that reads the temperature inside food; the only reliable way to know it is cooked safely
the deepest, densest spot in a piece of food, away from bone, where it cooks last

look.title: Where Does the Probe Go?
look.text: On the counter: a whole roasted chicken, a thin turkey burger in a skillet, a pork chop with the bone in, and a casserole dish of baked egg and cheese. Each needs a temperature check before it is served.
look.prompt: For each food, say exactly where you would put the thermometer probe and what mistake you are avoiding.

check.q: Where do you put the thermometer probe in a bone-in pork chop?
choices: In the thickest part of the meat, away from the bone
check.why: Bone gives a false high reading; the thickest part away from bone is the last spot to cook.

check.q: The juices from a chicken thigh run clear. What do you know?
choices: Nothing for sure; only a thermometer reading tells you
check.why: Color and juices are unreliable signs. Only a thermometer reading proves a safe temperature.

check.q: How do you check that a thermometer reads correctly?
choices: Hold it in the air and see if it matches the room
Compare it to the oven dial
Put it in ice water and look for 32 °F
check.why: A glass of ice water is 32 °F; a good thermometer reads that, and many can be adjusted if it does not.

lessons.title: Safe Minimum Temperatures
lessons.mainIdea: Every food has a safe minimum internal temperature; poultry is 165 °F, ground meat 160 °F, whole cuts and fish 145 °F.
reading: Here are the numbers, and they are worth memorizing. Poultry of every kind, whole, pieces or ground: 165 °F. Ground beef, pork, lamb and veal: 160 °F. Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal, such as steaks, chops and roasts: 145 °F, followed by a three-minute *rest* before cutting. Fish: 145 °F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes with a fork. Egg dishes: 160 °F, and plain eggs cooked until the yolk and white are firm. Leftovers and casseroles reheated: 165 °F.

Why is ground meat higher than a steak? On a whole steak, bacteria live on the outside surface, which hits high heat first. Grinding mixes the outside all through the inside, so the center of a burger needs to reach 160 °F. A burger cooked to 145 °F is not safe just because a steak at 145 °F is. Poultry carries Salmonella so often that its number is the highest of all.

The three-minute rest for whole cuts is part of the cooking, not a suggestion. Take the roast out at 145 °F, cover it loosely with foil and leave it three minutes. The heat inside keeps working, and the juices settle so they do not run out when you slice. Reheating is easy to forget: leftovers must reach 165 °F all the way through, so stir them halfway and check the center, not the edge.

Microwaves cook unevenly, leaving cold spots where bacteria survive. Cover the food, stir or rotate it partway through, and let it stand a minute before checking the temperature. When a package says "cook until steaming hot," that is a rough guide. The thermometer is the real test, and 165 °F is the real target.

words.d: the lowest temperature at the center of a food that kills harmful bacteria
letting cooked meat sit a few minutes after it leaves the heat; whole cuts rest three minutes after 145 °F

look.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
rows: beef, pork, lamb, veal whole cuts (then rest 3 min)
look.cite: USDA safe minimum internal temperature chart
look.prompt: A burger and a steak both read 150 °F. One is safe and one is not. Which is which, and why?

check.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for a chicken breast?
check.why: All poultry, whole or ground, must reach 165 °F.

check.q: Why must a hamburger reach 160 °F when a steak only needs 145 °F?
choices: Grinding mixes surface bacteria all through the meat
Beef in burgers is lower quality
check.why: Grinding spreads the bacteria from the surface into the center, so the center needs 160 °F.

check.q: A pork roast reads 145 °F. What comes next?
choices: Let it rest three minutes before slicing
Put it in the fridge to stop the cooking
check.why: Whole cuts of pork are safe at 145 °F followed by a three-minute rest.

lessons.title: Thawing Safely
lessons.mainIdea: Thaw frozen food in the fridge, in cold water changed every 30 minutes, or in the microwave, never on the counter.
reading: A frozen chicken sits on the counter all day so it will be ready for dinner. By afternoon the outside has been in the danger zone for hours while the middle is still ice. That is the problem with counter thawing: the surface, where bacteria live, warms up first and stays warm longest. The counter is never a safe place to thaw meat, poultry or fish.

There are three safe ways. The first is the *refrigerator*. Put the frozen food on a plate on the bottom shelf and let the fridge do the work. It is slow, about a day for a package of chicken pieces and longer for a large roast, so plan ahead. Food thawed this way can stay in the fridge a day or two before cooking and can even be refrozen, though it may lose some quality.

The second is *cold water*. Seal the food in a leakproof bag, submerge it in cold tap water, and change the water every 30 minutes so it stays cold. A pound of meat takes about an hour; larger packages take longer. Cook the food right away once it thaws. The third is the microwave on its defrost setting, which warms parts of the food into the danger zone, so cook it immediately afterward.

You can also skip thawing. Frozen meat and poultry can go straight into the oven or onto the stove; it just takes about half again as long to cook, and you must still check it with a thermometer. What you cannot do is leave it in the sink, in hot water, or on the counter and hope.

words.d: the safest way to thaw: frozen food on a plate on the bottom shelf of the fridge, planned a day ahead
thawing sealed food under cold water changed every 30 minutes, then cooking it at once

look.title: Dinner Is in Four Hours
look.text: It is 2 p.m. A two-pound package of frozen ground beef needs to become tacos by 6 p.m. Someone suggests putting it in the sink in hot water. Someone else says to leave it on the counter. A third person says the microwave. A fourth says cold water in a bag.
look.prompt: Pick the safe options, reject the unsafe ones with the reason, and say what must happen right after each safe method.

check.q: Which is a safe way to thaw a frozen chicken?
choices: In the sink in hot water
In a bowl of cold water changed every 30 minutes
On the porch on a cool day
check.why: Cold-water thawing in a sealed bag with the water changed every 30 minutes keeps the surface out of the danger zone.

check.q: Why is counter thawing unsafe?
choices: The surface warms into the danger zone while the middle is still frozen
check.why: The outside of the food spends hours between 40 and 140 °F, where bacteria multiply.

check.q: Meat was thawed in the microwave. What must happen next?
choices: Put it in the fridge for later
check.why: Microwave thawing warms parts of the food into the danger zone, so it must be cooked immediately.

lessons.title: Cooling and Storing Leftovers
lessons.mainIdea: Get leftovers into the fridge within two hours, in shallow containers, and use them within about three to four days.
reading: Dinner is over and a big pot of chili is still on the stove. The old advice was to let it cool before it goes in the fridge, but a deep pot of hot chili can take many hours to cool, all of it in the danger zone. The rule now is the two-hour rule again: leftovers go into the fridge within two hours of cooking, and warm food is fine to put in.

The trick is *shallow containers*. Divide the chili into containers no more than about two inches deep so the cold reaches the middle quickly. Leave the lids loose until it stops steaming, then seal. Label each with the food and the date. Do not stack hot containers on top of one another; give them room for cold air to move.

Use refrigerated leftovers within about three to four days. If you will not eat them by then, freeze them; frozen food stays safe for a long time, though quality fades. Reheat leftovers to 165 °F, stirring so there are no cold spots. Reheat only what you will eat; food that has been reheated and cooled more than once has spent extra time in the danger zone.

A clean, cold fridge is the last piece. Wipe up spills right away. Do not pack it so full that air cannot move, because a crowded fridge has warm pockets. Keep a thermometer inside and check it: 40 °F or below. When you are not sure how old something is or whether it was handled safely, the rule is short and worth repeating: when in doubt, throw it out.

words.d: a storage container about two inches deep or less, so hot food cools quickly in the fridge
cooked food saved after a meal; chill within two hours, use within three to four days, reheat to 165 °F

look.title: Leftover Rules by the Numbers

look.cite: USDA leftovers and food safety guidance
look.prompt: A pot of soup is put in the fridge whole, four inches deep, five hours after dinner. Which numbers were broken?

check.q: A big pot of chili is done at 6 p.m. By when must it be in the fridge?
choices: The next morning, once it is fully cool
check.why: The two-hour rule applies to leftovers; from 6 p.m. that means 8 p.m.

check.q: Why divide hot food into shallow containers?
choices: So the cold reaches the middle quickly
check.why: Shallow containers, about two inches deep, let food cool through quickly instead of sitting in the danger zone.

check.q: To what temperature should leftovers be reheated?
check.why: Reheated leftovers must reach 165 °F all the way through.

review.q: Which range is the danger zone?
Perishable food sat out at a picnic where the air was 88 °F. What is its limit?
review.why: At 88 °F the air is below 90 °F, so the normal two-hour limit applies.

review.q: What is the safe minimum internal temperature for ground turkey?
review.why: Ground turkey is poultry, and all poultry must reach 165 °F.

review.q: Which fridge arrangement follows the separate rule?
choices: Raw chicken on the bottom shelf in a container, salad above it
Raw chicken on the top shelf, salad below it
Raw chicken in the crisper drawer with the lettuce
review.why: Raw meat goes on the bottom shelf so drips cannot land on ready-to-eat food.

review.q: A cook rinses raw chicken in the sink before cooking. What is the problem?
choices: Splashing spreads bacteria over the sink and counter
The rinse washes away the seasoning
review.why: Rinsing raw poultry splashes bacteria around; cooking to 165 °F kills them without rinsing.

review.q: A steak reads 145 °F on the thermometer. What is the next step?
choices: Rest it three minutes, then serve
review.why: Whole cuts of beef are safe at 145 °F with a three-minute rest.

review.q: Which thawing method is NOT safe?
choices: In the refrigerator on a plate
In cold water changed every 30 minutes
In the microwave, then cooked at once
On the counter for the afternoon
review.why: Counter thawing leaves the surface in the danger zone for hours.

review.q: Leftover rice cooked at 6 p.m. should be in the fridge by when, and in what kind of container?
choices: Whenever it is cold, in a deep bowl
review.why: Leftovers go in within two hours in shallow containers so they cool through quickly.
